articles.title: Nvidia CEO steps down. And, Sen. Chris Van Hollen to run for majority leader
articles.summary: Nvidia's chief financial officer has been appointed interim CEO after Jensen Huang stepped down from the role. And, Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge Chuck Schumer for majority leader.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down following reports of his extramarital affairs, the company's board announced. The company's chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has been appointed interim CEO. The company launched an investigation after allegations surfaced that Huang had an affair with one of its clients, who U.S. intelligence officials concluded had been recruited by China's top spy agency. In an email to Nvidia staff, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife and promised to cooperate with the investigation. Nvidia's share price fell sharply Wednesday after the news of his second affair with an Nvidia executive came to light. Huang was widely considered an important business leader in the U.S. and had close ties to President Trump.

White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have been busy this week working on a new security framework between Russia and Europe and seeking to end the war in Ukraine. They led peace talks in Abu Dhabi, met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and then traveled to Ireland to meet with Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has announced he will challenge New York's Chuck Schumer for the Senate majority leader position. Following recent midterm victories, Van Hollen said voters desired a "change from the status quo." Elected to the Senate in 2016 after more than a decade in the House, the 67-year-old progressive gained national attention last year for lobbying for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia after his wrongful deportation to a prison in El Salvador. His announcement comes as progressive activists and some Democrats push for the 75-year-old Schumer's replacement. Schumer has been in the role since 2017 but faced criticism from the Democratic base for failing to confront Trump vigorously during a funding dispute in early 2025.

It's once again time to plan your Friendsgiving or Thanksgiving. You might be wondering: should you stick with your classic turkey recipe or spice things up? What about decorations — mini gourds or a stunning sunflower centerpiece? Let Life Kit help you decide with some fresh ideas to bring flavor, color and a touch of calm to your gathering.

Spice up your menu with new crowd-pleasing Thanksgiving recipes, including a salt-and-pepper roast turkey breast and pull-apart garlic bread. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.
Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Gentle Monster follows a loving couple who move to a farmhouse and whose peace shatters when the husband is accused of a crime. Léa Seydoux, who plays the wife named Lucy, discusses her first "complex" lead role in English with Morning Edition.
📺 TV: The new show Cupertino follows two Silicon Valley lawyers whose new firm represents the underdog, takes on big tech and grapples with the complexities of AI.

📚 Books: Journalist Mona Chalabi spent five years following 10 Americans of different economic standings to uncover what it takes to feel financially secure. Her book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, delves into the elusive nature of financial security.
🎵 Music: Rappers Lil Baby, Jack Harlow and SOB x RBE offer three ways to relight a flickering star and chart a path toward creative restoration through their respective albums, released today.

🎭 Theater: School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play wraps up its Broadway run this week. To celebrate, it will have paid livestreams on The League of Live Stream Theater's website. Set in a 1986 Ghanaian boarding school, the play humorously tackles themes of girlhood and beauty standards.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is out. An AI expert explains what his exit could mean for the AI boom
articles.summary: AI expert Gary Marcus breaks down what's at stake for Nvidia and the mess its new CEO has inherited.
body: A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.

Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.
"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told Morning Edition.

He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.
"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.
Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.
Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.
He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.
"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.

articles.title: U.S. envoys meet with Putin in the Kremlin after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to the Kremlin to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin and are scheduled to fly later to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
body: MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.
The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.

Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.
The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

But Moscow doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent.

Many in Europe see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the trans-Atlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.
Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, Kushner said in Moscow.

Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate targets. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," he said.

He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.
Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.

Zelenskyy said political changes, including Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following midterm elections and balloting in France next year, could bring "a window of opportunity" for a peace deal.
"The political landscape in Europe could change in 2027. … We also see changes already taking place in the United States," Zelenskyy said in Dublin late Wednesday.
He called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace.
Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement.
Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.

Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."

Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.

Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.

Military units have recorded "significant disruptions," including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.
Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.
Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.
Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn't be used for offensive strikes against Russia.

Zelenskyy said in Dublin that the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on. "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he said.

A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's main criminal investigation agency. It didn't identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.
Several senior Russian military officers have been killed by bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

articles.title: Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
articles.summary: Raka is the son of former President Joko Widodo. The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
body: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.
Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.

"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.
"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.

Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.
Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.

Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.

"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."

Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.
"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.

Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.

The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.

Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.

Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.
Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.
Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.

"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

articles.title: Colom wins Mississippi Senate race. And, White House warns Dems over future probes
articles.summary: After more than a week of counting ballots, Scott Colom has narrowly won the Mississippi Senate seat. And, the White House has sent a letter warning Democrats who plan to investigate the administration.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Democrat Scott Colom has won the U.S. Senate seat from Mississippi, defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just a few thousand votes. Colom will be the first Black Senator from the state in nearly 150 years. His win expands the Democratic majority in the new Congress to 55 seats. The Alaska race is still undecided.

The White House is warning Democrats that their planned investigations into administration officials could cross the line into "blatant criminality." White House Counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee next year, that the administration is monitoring "abusive and capricious threats" from Democrats. The letter concludes by saying that "the administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process, motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government." Garcia said Democrats will not be deterred by threats from the Department of Justice or Trump's lawyers.

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a significant prisoner swap after two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi. Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are now in Moscow today to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and attempt to make more headway to end the war in Ukraine.

Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.

Abdul El-Sayed has made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. The 42-year-old progressive from Michigan is already calling for a new direction for his party and urging President Trump to collaborate on actionable solutions. El-Sayed said that voters have temporarily entrusted Democrats with power, but warns that they risk losing that trust if they don't act boldly. As the senator-elect comes into the new role, he is advocating for new Democratic leadership in Congress, an end to the war in Iran, the passage of "Medicare for All" and the abolishment of ICE. While he acknowledges the challenge Senate Democrats face with a majority that's a few seats shy of being filibuster-proof, he remains open to working with his new Republican colleagues. In conversation with Morning Edition's Leila Fadel, El-Sayed reflects on the recent elections, the future of the Democratic Party and the need for impactful legislation in the upcoming years.

articles.title: Why is the Microsoft outage lasting so long?
articles.summary: Microsoft says it is seeing "improvements" following a global outage but efforts to fully resume services are ongoing.
body: Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage
A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, courts and governments around the world, with users struggling to access emails and artificial intelligence products.
Efforts to completely resume services remain ongoing after issues were first experienced on Thursday.
Microsoft said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.
The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".
In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".
The company attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.
The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.
In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.

Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".
In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.
Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".
The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.
When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.
Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.

articles.title: Scandal-hit Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits, plunging AI chipmaking giant into turmoil
articles.summary: US lawmakers now want to question him over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
body: Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation

Jensen Huang has abruptly quit as chief executive of AI chipmaking giant Nvidia after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill.
Nvidia is now under scrutiny from US lawmakers in Washington DC demanding Huang answer questions over whether one of his alleged relationships was with a Chinese spy.
One of the world's most valuable companies as a result of the AI boom, Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, called an emergency meeting of her executive team to discuss the company's future.
His alleged conduct not only potentially crossed professional boundaries, but has made Nvidia the target of questions from US politicians who have expressed concern about national security risks.
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.
And US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.
Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons, along with other Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, publicly demanded that Huang brief Congress on the matter.
If he refuses to appear voluntarily before any committee that calls him, he could be subpoenaed, one Senate staff member told the BBC.
Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.
Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.
Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.
Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.
Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.

But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.
He is far from the first tech titan to become embroiled in revelations of infidelity.
Bill Gates of Microsoft and Jeff Bezos of Amazon had affairs exposed in the last decade. Both men are now divorced from their wives.
Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.
Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.
Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.
Because of Nvidia's size and success in recent years, such a drop can have a direct impact on the savings accounts of ordinary Americans.
Nvidia's value makes up about 7% of the S&P 500 index. That index is offered as a popular index fund in US retirement savings accounts.
Those account balances rise and fall with the changes of the stock market.

articles.title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president says it makes sense for European leaders to be involved as Ukraine hopes to eventually join the EU.
body: US envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (right) met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.

Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.

Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.

"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.

Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

articles.title: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site
articles.summary: It says it has never been able to visit a uranium enrichment plant at Isfahan which Iran announced over a year ago.
body: The nuclear agency has not been able to inspect any sites attacked by the US and Israel last year
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.

Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.
In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.
Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.
Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.
Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.
The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.
The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.

"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.
Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.
Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.

The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.

The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

articles.title: African Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
articles.summary: Hall has been seeking a US visa in South Africa as other African beauty queens face similar hurdles.
body: Roseanna Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by US visa restrictions
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.
Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.
"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.
Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.

Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.
"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.
Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.
In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.

"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.
Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.
The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.
Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.
"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.
Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."
In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.
She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"
The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

articles.title: Nigerian university in mourning after four students die at post-exam party
articles.summary: The university has banned all parties, while investigations are underway to find the cause of the students' deaths.
body: All parties have been banned at the university
Four Nigerian students have died after attending a party in the south-eastern town of Nsukka to celebrate the end of their final exams.
The cause of death has not been confirmed but police spokesman Daniel Ndukwe said the two men and two women had reportedly fallen ill after consuming alcoholic drinks at the party.
The University of Nigeria Nsukka has declared three days of mourning, during which academic and social activities will be suspended.
The tragedy comes amid a wider crackdown on fake and adulterated alcoholic drinks in Nigeria, where the food and drug regulator has been raiding suspected producers of unsafe food and beverages.

The university's Vice-Chancellor, Professor Simon Ortuanya, said the university had received a distress call at 22:00 on Wednesday, and sent security personnel to a house party at Praise Lodge, outside the campus in Nsukka's Hilltop area.
"The preliminary investigation and interim report point to alleged alcohol abuse or drug paraphernalia and things like that. But we are not conclusive on those matters," he said.
He described the deaths as "tragic and painful".
"As a community, we mourn, not just alone, we mourn with the families, the parents that have suffered these years to train the men and women in their studies," he said.
Ortuanya also announced a ban on signing-out celebrations, which are commonly held by final-year students to mark the completion of their studies.

The celebrations often involve parties, dancing, photographs and friends signing one another's shirts. He urged students to use graduation as a time to reflect on their university experience and prepare for life beyond campus.
The university said it was working with security agencies to establish what had caused the deaths.
The police have also launched an investigation. They said alcoholic drinks had been recovered from the scene and the bodies taken to a mortuary for autopsies.
The investigation comes amid wider concerns about unsafe alcoholic drinks in Nigeria.
In September, dozens of people fell ill after consuming locally made alcoholic drinks and herbal mixtures in communities across Ondo State, south-west Nigeria.
More than 11 people died in the Araromi-Obu area, while more than 50 others were hospitalised.
Investigations found that some of the drinks had been contaminated with methanol, a highly toxic form of alcohol that can cause blindness and death.
Nigeria's food and drug regulator, Nafdac, reported more than 150 cases, including 48 confirmed deaths. More than 80 people were hospitalised, and five lost their sight.
The regulator has been carrying out raids across the country, targeting facilities suspected of producing fake or adulterated alcoholic drinks, food and beverages.
Nigeria has long struggled with the sale of unsafe and adulterated products, which campaigners warn pose a serious threat to public health.

articles.title: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
articles.summary: More than 900 victims are thought to have fallen prey to the FaceStealer scheme in the last 18 months.
body: FBI redacted examples of the 900 victim videos secretly recorded by North Korean hackers
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.

Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.

According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.

A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".

"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

articles.title: Hegseth awards medal to war memorial guard who reprimanded him and group
articles.summary: Specialist Thomas Iglesias was given a Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties after Wednesday's incident.
body: US Army guard reprimands group that includes US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at Arlington National Cemetery.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery.

A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet.
In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier".
Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias.

He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads.

In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Hegseth (right) awarded the medal to Specialist Thomas Iglesias after being reprimanded by him
The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell later said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured - and will always honour - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and First Lady Melania Trump bow their heads in prayer during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery
Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.

During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.
"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."
Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.

Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill.
Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

articles.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: The attack is thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an open stretch of the Baltic Sea.
body: The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.

The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.

Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.

Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.

"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.

Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.

Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.

Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

articles.title: Australian footballers will not be charged after hotel incident, police say
articles.summary: Four Sydney Swans players had been under investigation after an alleged sexual assault after a game in Melbourne.
body: Isaac Heeney is among the players police say will not be charged over an incident at a hotel in August
Four top Australian Football League (AFL) players who were investigated in relation to an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne earlier this year will not be charged, police have said.
After a "thorough investigation and based on legal advice" police would not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence", police said in a statement.
Four Sydney Swans players - Isaac Heeney, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who now plays for North Melbourne - had been suspended for the rest of the season over the incident in August.
The men previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards by inviting women back to the hotel after a game and drinking.

Australian media reported that three women, understood to be adult entertainers, had alleged inappropriate touching during the incident at the Pullman Hotel and are reportedly looking into civil action.
"Due to the ongoing civil matter, Victoria Police is unable to make further comment," police said in a statement on Friday.
A fifth player, Riley Bice, who was also suspended by the club, had already been cleared by police.
Heeney welcomed the police announcement, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult for my family, [my fiancee] Steffie and those close to me".
"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice," he continued.

articles.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself.
body: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.
Now the political pressure is building.
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?
Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?

articles.title: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
articles.summary: Claims the entire Australian team knew of the 2018 sandpaper cheating plot are dividing the cricket world.
body: Pat Cummins spent over an hour fielding questions over sandpapergate on Friday

As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.
Josh says he was surprised the scandal is back in the news

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja has said he owed it to the three players punished to tell his side of the story
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.
"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."
However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Australia kicked off it's summer with an ODI against England on Friday
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.
"I don't know what the outcome will be."

articles.title: Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state
articles.summary: Alaskans are still waiting for the full results, including in the close Senate race between Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.
body: The results of the Alaska midterm elections might not be known until 18 November
For the last few weeks, in addition to its usual payload of passengers, medicine, and supplies, Alaska Seaplanes has carried some unique cargo: ballots.

The regional airline is a piece of a complex logistical puzzle that sees Alaskans' midterms elections votes cast by mail and in person carried across the vast expanse of America's largest state, which is primarily connected by water and air rather than roads.

This considerable task explains why, a week after most US states knew their results in the midterms - in which the Democrats won back both chambers of Congress from the Republicans - Alaskans are still waiting for the Senate race to be called.

The victor in this close contest between the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, former congresswoman Mary Peltola, could remain unknown until 18 November, when officials expect to have counted all eligible ballots.

"We do feel a sense of pride of making sure we do the job right - the really complicated job of getting all these ballots across thousands of miles in Alaska," Andy Kline, the marketing director of Alaska Seaplanes, which serves the south-eastern part of the state, told the BBC.
"We feel like we're part of the last leg of that journey of those ballots."
An Alaska Seaplanes aircraft similar to the ones that transport ballots, along with other cargo and mail, during elections

Some precincts in Alaska are able to communicate their initial results to centralised election offices on election night, allowing state officials and news outlets to report some preliminary vote tallies.
But it takes time for the full picture of how people have voted to emerge.

As well as having the logistical challenge of counting votes from across a state more than six times the size of the UK, there is a delay waiting for mail ballots to arrive, says Charles Stewart, an election expert at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
These are allowed to arrive up to 10 days later, or 15 days for overseas voters, if postmarked by election day.
Stewart said that election officials had "chosen to err on the side of getting it right rather than a rush to report the second and third tranches of ballots that get counted".
Regardless of whether ballots were cast in person or by mail, all of them eventually wind up in the state capital of Juneau – which is only reachable by plane or boat – for scanning and counting.
While more urban districts can get their materials on a plane late on election night, it takes longer for smaller or more remote parts of Alaska.

In some places, "you get someone who's basically running the election for their family and their neighbours because it's such a small village", says Scott Kendall, an election lawyer who previously worked on two campaigns for Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski.
In these smaller areas, ballots are sealed up in special envelopes or containers and sent it through the mail - which is where companies like Alaska Seaplanes comes in.
Ballots are put on the planes and sent to Juneau, where they then get dropped at the post office and delivered.
"It's part of our daily routine, just another couple of boxes," Kline said.
Former congresswoman Mary Peltola is the Democratic candidate
Once all the in-person and absentee mail ballots reach Juneau, election officials will complete their review.

If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote in the first round, officials will quickly use ranked-choice voting to re-allocate votes from the lowest-scoring candidates to their voters' second choices.
Then Alaska will finally declare a winner for its Senate race, as well as contests for governor and US House of Representatives.

Adding to the suspense of who will win the Senate race is the question of whether another Republican candidate called Dan Sullivan, who was allegedly recruited by Democratic operatives, would affect the outcome. Results released so far suggest a low probability.

This week, President Donald Trump alleged Alaska's Senate election had been "rigged" due to the second Sullivan's involvement. His administration is appealing its rejected lawsuit to halt certification of the election over the issue, which a lower court dismissed.
US Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska is one of two men with the same name who were on the ballot
Meanwhile, a judge has denied an attempt by Peltola's campaign to get information about how many absentee ballots election officials rejected, as well as information about those voters.
The state argued it had no obligation to share this data, and doing so would violate voter privacy.
While the result of the election is of the greatest importance to many, for people like Kline, the process is also key.
"We're all citizens," he said of himself and his colleagues.
"We all feel like we have skin in the game to make sure that our elections are accurate and timely."
