articles.title: More than 60% of Germany’s female soldiers report harassment or abuse
articles.summary: Defence minister says extent of sexual misconduct found by study is ‘unacceptable’, as military tries to attract more recruits
body: Germany’s defence minister has promised a “zero tolerance” approach to sexual abuse in the armed forces after a study found soldiers, particularly women, faced extensive harassment within the ranks.

The first comprehensive study of its kind into the Bundeswehr, conducted by the Centre for Military History and Social Sciences in Potsdam and released this week, comes as the military is trying to attract new recruits in response to global threats.

It found that more than 60% of female soldiers had reported experiencing some form of sexual harassment or abuse while on duty, ranging from sexually explicit remarks and degrading rituals to sexual violence.

Nearly 40% of the 4,000 women who responded to the survey said they had been addressed with suggestive comments and sexualised remarks, while 15% reported being harassed with mobile phone pictures taken against their will and in some cases altered using AI.
Just over 8% reported having been physically attacked, and 2% said they had been the victims of sexual violence.
Around 19% of male ‌soldiers had experienced a similar form of sexual misconduct, with non-binary or gay soldiers disproportionately affected, the study found.

Boris Pistorius, the defence minister, said the figures were “unacceptable”, in particular for a military that is trying to considerably increase its numbers. The Bundeswehr has pumped billions into boosting both personnel and equipment. Military bosses have set a target of 260,000 active-duty troops and 200,000 reservists by 2035, in the hope of avoiding the introduction of conscription.

Pistorius said he was struck by the finding that women in units with a higher proportion of other women were less frequently affected, which he said “argues in favour of recruiting more women into the Bundeswehr”.

He said he had been advised by some colleagues to ditch the study, over fears it would sully the reputation of the military. To do so, he said, would be akin to “turning a blind eye”, which in the long term would do more damage to the Bundeswehr. The study would be repeated every year, he added.
“Zero tolerance applies to sexual harassment within the Bundeswehr,” the minister said.

Pistorius expressed concern over a high level of reluctance to report incidents. About a third of those surveyed said they did not or would not report incidents because of a lack of trust in what their superiors would do.
Before the study results were made public, Pistorius set up a hotline this month, meant to serve military personnel, which is to be staffed around the clock, and is called HELP.

In future, Pistorius said, those who made complaints should receive more information about the status of their proceedings, after victims said they were often left in the dark, but expected to continue serving.

The ministry said that, of 45,000 active or former members of the armed forces contacted to participate in the survey, 18% responded. It said its analysis showed that the figures were nevertheless representative.

articles.title: ‘The time is ripe’: ex-helicopter engineer poised to be Germany’s first female president
articles.summary: Backed by MPs from across the political divide, Bavarian Ilse Aigner offers an approachability and warmth the chancellor lacks
body: Germany has had 12 presidents since the end of the second world war, all of them men. Now, for the first time, the federal republic is on the brink of getting a female head of state. But Ilse Aigner, the lead candidate for the post, is unusual in more ways than one.
“No law degree. No marriage. No penis,” is how the left-leaning Taz newspaper put it this week – a wry, if blunt, assessment of what a break with history the 61-year-old Bavarian represents.
Friedrich Merz, Germany’s Christian Democrat (CDU) chancellor, put Aigner forward as his candidate this week after months of speculation, saying it was “high time” a woman took up the role.

If elected in January, Aigner will succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier in what is a largely ceremonial role but nonetheless Germany’s highest state position. And as she has the backing not only of Merz’s CDU but his Social Democrat partners and the opposition Greens, little is standing in her way.

Some are delighted. Jörg Thadeusz, a liberal writer and popular TV presenter with a penchant for satire, has taken his enthusiasm for Aigner so far as to have the name Ilse tattooed on his upper left arm. Pictures of him revealing the tattoo on TV this week made headline news, as media talked of the Aigner-Welle (Aigner wave) to describe the unexpected ripple of enthusiasm for the Catholic Bavarian – among the political establishment, at least.

“Ilse Aigner is … a candidate who right now could really do Germany some good,” said Thadeusz. Unlike far-right populists who were polarising the country with their demands for “Deutschland First”, he said, Aigner embraced a form of Heimat (homeland) that was “neither folklore nor a political battle cry”.

Not everyone shares his enthusiasm. Aigner’s relationship with the populist Alternative für Deutschland, the largest opposition force in the Bundestag, got off to a tricky start this week after she turned down their demand to present herself to them as a candidate. Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader and the most prominent woman in German politics, accused Aigner of failing to respect “democratic culture and manners” as well as “the millions of voters we represent”.

Despite having held a cabinet position, as agriculture minister from 2008 to 2013 under Angela Merkel, Aigner is not a household name. She began in local politics 30 years ago and entered the Bundestag in 1998. Instead of the usually prerequisite degree, she has a vocational qualification as an electrical engineer with a speciality in manufacturing helicopters, her job before entering politics.
“She’s the first head of state of the Federal Republic of Germany who can personally repair a government helicopter,” Thadeusz quipped this week.

In her nomination speech this week, Aigner said she hoped to inspire aspirational Germans: “As the first woman in the highest state office, I would stand with my person and my background as a symbol of the promise of upward mobility in our country.”

Aigner has spoken openly about surviving two serious tumour diagnoses – one in her spinal cord when she was 17, and thyroid cancer in her 40s, when she was a minister – saying they had given her perspective as a politician.

Now feted by the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to the CDU, she once struggled to be recognised. Her attempts in the early 90s, aged 27, to become mayor of her birth town, Feldkirchen-Westerham, south-east of Munich, failed because she was unmarried, which the party of arch-conservatives said was “too unclear a condition” and made her unsuitable to serve.

She still lives in Feldkirchen-Westerham, a Bavarian town of 10,000 people, where her parents ran an electronics shop. There she shares a house on a 1970s estate living under one roof with three generations of her family, including her three older sisters and their offspring. Local people refer to her affectionally as “die Ilse” (equivalent to “the Ilse”, or “our Ilse”), and describe her as being a regular attender at town celebrations. She typically cycles, “whether to the butchers and bakers, or to the opening of a new windfarm”, one resident said.

For Merz the chance to back the first female presidency is a chance to shed his reputation as a Frauenfeind (misogynist), an image that goes back in part to his decades-long rivalry with Merkel, but has been underscored to some extent by his leadership style in office. In an editorial this week, the Münchner Merkur noted that Aigner’s perceived strengths neatly complemented the chancellor’s deficiencies: “Her approach compensates for what Merz lacks: approachability, popularity, a warmth that can absorb the effects of polarisation.”

Merkel was regarded as a powerful female trailblazer not just in Germany but around the world. She was referred to at home as “Mutti” – both a term of affection and patronisingly used to describe her supposedly maternal stewardship of the country. Five years after her departure from the political stage, feminist commenters hope Aigner might prove a symbolic boost.

“The time is ripe for a woman. We have such an under-representation of women in society, in politics, in business, and it’s high time a woman held this highest office in the land. I’m very happy about that,” said Britta Hasselmann, a leading Green MP, in a podcast interview this week.

But even more important, Hasselmann emphasised, was the extent to which Aigner might draw together a country deeply divided by ideological rifts and economic tensions, where extremists are snapping at the heels of the political centre. The presidency needed someone “who can unite people, especially in such polarised times, who is empathetic, down to earth, and who tries to send a strong signal that common ground is valued in a democracy. And I believe she is capable of that,” Hasselmann said.

articles.title: ‘El Niño turned off the taps’: factors behind Indonesia’s wildfires revealed
articles.summary: Country’s fiercest fires in at least a decade produced toxic smog related to 400,000 respiratory infections
body: Indonesia’s fiercest fires in at least a decade were amplified by an “El Niño that turned off the taps” and “fossil fuels that turned up the heat”, scientists have revealed.

Along with the conversion of forests to plantations, this created the conditions for blazes that have burned almost 3m hectares (7.4m acres) – 19 times the size of Greater London – this year, and cast a choking haze across much of south-east Asia.

An international team of World Weather Attribution scientists analysed the different elements of this triple whammy in Java, Kalimantan and Sumatra to assess how each affected the peak fire season from August to October.
They found global heating, primarily driven by the burning of oil, gas and coal, raised temperatures by 1.6C in this three-month period, drying the land and vegetation.
On top of this, El Niño, which is on course to break all records, added a further 0.3C and reduced rainfall by about 50%.
“El Niño turned off the taps, but fossil fuel emissions turned up the heat,” Prof Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.

“We know that as the world continues to warm, fire weather during El Niño years will become increasingly severe. Without rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels and strengthened land-management protections, we will see more and much worse fire seasons like this in the future.”
Furthermore, they learned the hot, dry air conditions were made three times more likely by climate change and five times more by El Niño.
Decades of logging, agroforestry expansion and peatland-draining also contributed to the tinderbox conditions.

“Indonesia landscapes have changed dramatically over the last 30 years with extensive pipeline drainage and deforestation creating a landscape that is extremely vulnerable to ignition,” said Pramudhian Firdaus, a meteorologist at Melbourne University, who also works with the Indonesian meteorological service.
Fires continue to burn in Indonesia, because El Niño has helped to delay the rainy season by 20 to 30 days, according to the country’s Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG).

The latest local reports indicate 2.88m hectares have been blackened in Indonesia so far in 2026. If confirmed, this would surpass the record for this century, which was set in 2015 when 2.6m hectares of land was burnt, generating 333m tonnes of carbon emissions.

Fires and drier than usual conditions around the world have contributed to an unusually large rise in the predicted CO2 emissions for 2027, despite a slight fall in pollution from fossil fuels as a result of the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
There have also been political implications, with protesters in Jakarta calling for the government to declare the fires a national emergency.

The health effects are still being calculated. Wildfire smoke has choked many cities in Indonesia, with at least 400,000 related respiratory infections, including 180,000 children, according to the health ministry. The toxic smog has spread as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.

Maja Vahlberg, technical adviser at the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, said: “The severe fires in Indonesia are leading to health impacts for people across the region with smoke especially affecting children, older adults and those with pre-existing conditions who tend to be more vulnerable …

“El Niño conditions – even with the extra boost from climate change – are highly predictable, which provides an opportunity for proactive, preventive action to stop future years from having impacts on this scale.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Europe to join negotiations, says Kushner, as Putin warns against peace keepers
articles.summary: Jared Kushner says move will allow talks to address ‘broader postwar European security arrangements’; Putin refuses to soften territorial demands. What we know on day 1,724
body: Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries, Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said late on Thursday, after meeting Russian president Vladimir Putin. “This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner ​said ​later on X. “We are also working toward ‌what would be the largest prisoner ​exchange of the war, potentially reuniting thousands of people ⁠with their families.”

After the Moscow meeting, Kushner and Witkoff flew ⁠to Ireland to attend a European summit and meet Zelenskyy, who said he was pleased at the prospect of European participation in talks and said he hoped the agenda would include steps towards a ceasefire and de-escalating the conflict. “We decided that we will work on an agenda about any kind of de-escalation, some kind of ceasefires,” Zelenskyy said after meeting the US envoys. “I hope that we will have such agenda,” he said.

Putin warned Europe not to send peacekeeping troops into Ukraine in the event of a peace deal saying it was a “continuation of war”. Putin also refused to soften his territorial demands and said Washington must work with its European allies to understand if they want peace or war in Ukraine.

Putin’s comments underlined how ⁠difficult the negotiations could become, given sharp differences between Moscow ​and European capitals over the way the war should end. “The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment because they are our partners and it’s important to us that they take part,” Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.

Kushner told Putin Washington had detected what he called “a big change” on the European side and was confident that expanding peace talks to include the Europeans would not hinder progress. Putin said Moscow had always been open to talking to the EU about Ukraine, but ​signalled serious outstanding differences. “As far as the Europeans are concerned, we have never been opposed to engaging in dialogue ‌with Europe, and we have never broken off that dialogue. It was ‌they who broke off the dialogue with the Russian Federation,” he said. “We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the US administration as a whole, to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” said Putin.

However, Zelenskyy said new restrictions were affecting the US-made satellite communications Kyiv uses on the battlefield, and that he found the US approach of discussing a new European security order with Russia “a bit strange”. Earlier on Thursday, he said disruptions to the Starshield satellite ​communications service had affected the entire frontline and Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine. Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service, and Ukraine suffered similar disruptions last month. “So far we know very little (on the Starshield restrictions). But some things are already clear: if someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then it tells us where things are going,” he said. SpaceX declined to comment.

During the talks, the conflict between the two countries continued. A Russian drone ⁠strike killed two people in the ⁠northern ⁠Ukrainian ​region of Sumy, Governor Oleh Hryhorov said ⁠on Telegram late on Thursday, while in Rivne ⁠in the north-west, ​five ‌people were injured ‌after a Russian drone hit ‌an apartment building, a local Ukrainian official said on Telegram early on Friday. In Russia’s ‌Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, a man ​was killed and another four injured in a drone attack, ⁠local officials said on Telegram ​on ​Thursday. Meanwhile, Ukrainian agricultural company Kernel Holding said on ⁠Thursday it had suspended operations at all its oilseed extraction plants ⁠following a ⁠series ​of Russian attacks on its facilities.

articles.title: Second world war ‘brain’ bunker in cliffs of Dover opens to public
articles.summary: The bunker, entered via a hatch in a field, controlled a gun battery used to attack German ships in Channel
body: It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.

The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. This acted as a “brain” for a gun battery that was used to defend Dover and attack German ships in the Channel, according to Jon Barker, who led the excavation project for the National Trust.
Barker was the first person to enter the bunker when it was rediscovered in 2017 after it had been secretly mothballed in 1957 and classified until 1981 owing to its military importance.

“It was a Tutankhamun moment for a conflict archaeologist,” he said. “We had done all this research on the people who had served there, and then suddenly you’re standing in their office. It was an exciting moment.”

The plotting room and the artillery it controlled can be directly traced to Churchill. Soon after his “fight them on the beaches” speech, he visited the Kent coast and was alarmed to observe enemy ships passing through the strait of Dover unchallenged.
At the same time, Dover was on the frontline of a Britain facing regular bombardment by enemy guns in occupied France.
In a July 1940 memo Churchill wrote: “We have to fight for command of the straits by artillery, to destroy the enemy batteries and fortify our own.”

He ordered the most advanced technology to be used and demanded weekly updates on progress on Dover’s new defences. The guns were ready within 100 days and the plotting room bunker was completed 64 days later.
“The guns were known around here as Churchill’s pets,” Barker said.

Physical traces of the urgency of the construction were still visible at the site, said Barker. He pointed to the rough openings through the walls and floors for the cabling. Contemporary accounts describe how the equipment was installed before drawings governing its layout were available.

The plotting room housed a 1.8-metre-long electromechanical computer known as a fire direction table. It was used to calculate the position of moving ships when shells hit and to send firing instructions to gun crews.

Barker said the discovery of the plotting room reminded him of the rescue of Bletchley Park, the codebreaking site in Buckinghamshire, in the 1990s. “We didn’t know about it then, but now it’s all part of our national consciousness,” he said. “The plotting room is a new hidden history.”

He added: “We tend to think of plotting tables as glamorous Wrens [members of the Women’s Royal Naval Service] pushing around markers on a map as they do in war films. But it’s not a map – it’s a really cutting edge electromechanical computer, and it is completely unique.”
The computer was deliberately destroyed in 1957 to stop it falling into enemy hands.
Up to 10 people at a time worked in the plotting room. Barker is keen to make contact with anyone who had family members who served there, to help him understand how the machine worked.
“What we know about it is based on a manual and ghost markings on the floor. I would really love to hear if anybody knows if their family members served at Fan Bay because the records are scant.”

The identities of only a handful of people who operated the computer are known. They include Wallas Eaton, an actor who later appeared as Senator Ludicrus Sextus in the TV comedy series Up Pompeii, alongside Frankie Howerd.
A man named WP Bryant, a lance bombardier, was also recorded as a plotter at Fan Bay. “He was a tailor so he probably had a head for numbers,” said Barker.

The plotting room, which from Friday can be visited via National Trust guided tours through a hatch in a field, has been preserved as Barker and his team found it. Remnants include old newspapers found on the floor, old shoes and official notices. There is also chalked graffiti on one of the service tunnels saying “heroes fan hole Dodds and Petitt”. Barker said Dodds and Petitt may have been involved in installing cables to the bunker.
“They were probably self-appointed heroes responsible for marshalling horrible thick cable through particularly uncomfortable tunnels,” he said.

“There’s something very special about standing in a place that has changed so little since the people who worked here left. Rather than recreate the past, we’ve carefully conserved the plotting room so visitors can experience it much as we found it, with all the marks of its history still visible. It’s a rare opportunity to discover a completely different side of the white cliffs.”

articles.title: Did Indonesia’s vice-president just resign because he didn’t have a high school diploma?
articles.summary: Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the son of former president Joko Widodo, has faced months of questions about his eligibility for office
body: It has been a turbulent few weeks in Indonesia, with claims the president’s phone was tapped, an uneasy political alliance seemingly in tatters, and now the vice-president resigning after a court ruled he never finished high school.
On the face of it, the drama centres on the educational achievements of vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka, but there is more to it than that.
Here we explain what happened, why and the deeper political machinations at play in the world’s third-largest democracy.
Gibran, 39, has for months faced questions about his education credentials, including most recently in Indonesia’s constitutional court.

Responding to a petition filed in an attempt to unseat him, the court ruled last month there was “no convincing evidence” that Gibran possessed a diploma, certificate or degree from abroad that could show he ever finished high school.

However, the court said it could not annul the results of the 2024 election, which saw him elected, even though Indonesian law stipulates that having a high school certificate is a prerequisite to run.
Gibran attended Orchid Park secondary school in Singapore and UTS Insearch in Australia, before earning a bachelor’s degree ​through the Management Development ​Institute of Singapore.
But this was not enough to quiet his critics.
The millennial leader has struggled to capture the heart of the masses like his father, the wildly popular former president, Joko Widodo, widely known by his nickname Jokowi.
Galvanised by the court ruling, this week the parliament intensified efforts to impeach him.
Gibran met president Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday and offered to resign.
By Wednesday evening, he had stepped down, according to a senior aide.
Gibran is a controversial figure, and not just because of his schooling.

Jokowi’s eldest son showed little interest in politics until he ran for mayor of Solo in 2019. Previously he ran several food related businesses, including one selling pancakes filled with chocolate and cheese.
When it was initially suggested he may run for vice-president, there was another eligibility requirement he did not pass: he wasn’t old enough.
However, before the registrations closed the constitutional court created a last-minute exception to the age limit, allowing candidates under 40 to run.

The chief justice of the court at the time was Anwar Usman, who was Gibran’s uncle and Jokowi’s brother in law. He was later found guilty of ethical violations for hearing the case despite the conflict of interest.
Anwar was removed but the ruling remained.
In short, it has a lot to do with the deteriorating relationship between Prabowo, a once-disgraced military general, and his predecessor Jokowi.

In 2019 and after a decade in power, Jokowi was looking for ways to continue his influence after stepping down. One way was through his eldest son Gibran, whom he guided onto Prabowo’s presidential ticket.
Prabowo, who had already lost the presidency twice to Jokowi, accepted Gibran as his vice presidential running mate knowing that he could leverage Jokowi’s popularity.
It worked and analysts later said his 2024 victory was in part due to the “Jokowi effect”.
But the alliance has always been tenuous.
Analysts said it was likely only a matter of time before it would break down, and that Gibran would be sidelined.
In another sign of a momentous split, last week it was alleged that Prabowo’s chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is a longtime Jokowi ally, had wiretapped the president’s phone.
Indonesian police said ⁠on Thursday they were investigating ⁠treason charges against ⁠four ​suspects in a case, including Listyo, who has not commented publicly about the allegations.
Things may continue to be rocky.
“I wouldn’t read this as a one-off resignation,” says political analyst Kennedy Muslim.
In the short term the People’s Consultative Assembly (MPR), Indonesia’s top legislative body, will choose the new vice-president from two names the president nominates, within 60 days of the vacancy.
The events will allow Prabowo to clear any Jokowi loyalists from his inner circle and consolidate power around his Gerindra party, but that also carries a risk.

“The more power concentrates in Prabowo and Gerindra, the more discontent has a single address,” says Muslim, noting that president’s popularity plummeted to 44.5% this October, down from 81.2% in November last year.
Facing streets protests, economic turbulence and dissatisfaction with his key policies, such as his free meals program, Prabowo has multiple challenges ahead.
“If his popularity keeps falling, coalition partners who look solid today will start hedging for 2029 behind his back,” says Muslim, of the next election.

articles.title: Putin takes hard line in US talks as Ukraine says Starlink disrupted again
articles.summary: Russian president says he would target any foreign troops sent to Ukraine and refuses to soften territorial demands
body: Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.

During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.

Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.

The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.
Related: Trump could be about to sell out Ukraine. Europe must get its act together, fast | Paul Taylor

Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.
The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.
Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join the talks in Berlin.

Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.
But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.

The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.
Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.
“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.

EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”
Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.

More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.

According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.
Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.

The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.
Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

articles.title: Pork fat, a heating pad and a five-storey jump: how a 74-year-old escaped house arrest in Argentina
articles.summary: Leonardo Bertulazzi, ex-member of Italy’s radical far-left Red Brigades, fled in dramatic fashion, ‘like something out of a movie’
body: As dozens of police and sniffer dogs poured into San Telmo, a traditional Buenos Aires neighbourhood with cobblestone streets, on Tuesday morning, one of the clerks at a shop selling dulce de leche asked them why. He said they were “looking for a bomb”.
It was only later that she found out there was no danger of being blown up after all, and that authorities were, in fact, hunting for a fugitive. “An Italian mafioso, right?” she asked.

The escapee was no mobster, exactly: he was Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, a former member of Italy’s radical far-left militant group the Red Brigades, who had been living under house arrest in Argentina after his arrest in 2024, awaiting extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year sentence.
On Tuesday, however, the 74-year-old escaped from house arrest in dramatic fashion.
“It was like something out of a movie,” said a person with knowledge of the investigation who asked to remain anonymous.

At around 6am, when most security forces “were focused on the Pope’s security” as the pontiff was visiting Argentina, Bertulazzi cut off his ankle monitor, the source said. In order to bypass its temperature and pressure sensors, Bertulazzi apparently wrapped it in a tube with pork fat and left it next to a heating pad.
He then rappelled down from his apartment’s fifth floor, jumped in to a vacant lot behind the building, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street.

Two weeks prior, an alert in the ankle monitor’s system had gone off, indicating that he might have been tinkering with the machine. On Tuesday, police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data entirely, and headed to the house – only to find him missing.
Related: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
“He knew exactly what he was doing”, said the source. “After all, he’s a guy who worked in logistics for the Italian brigade.”

Indeed, Bertulazzi once held a senior position in the Red Brigades, an organization responsible for a series of attacks throughout the 1970s, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.

He had been sentenced in absentia on terrorism charges in Italy in 1985 and 1997 and was living in Argentina in 2002 when, after years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities. He was freed a few months later, and in 2004 he secured refugee status. But it was revoked two years ago, and he was arrested again and put under house arrest, for health concerns. Italy’s rightwing prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, framed the move as a significant political win made possible by her government’s close relations with Argentina’s president, Javier Milei.

After he fled, Italy’s interior ministry undersecretary, Wanda Ferro, said Argentinian police were responsible because they were “supposed to ensure surveillance and the handover [of Bertulazzi] to the Italian authorities”, and urged his swift reapprehension. On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture.

The Italian press has reacted to the escape with bemusement, noting his ability to abseil from a fifth-floor balcony despite the 74-year-old’s supposedly poor health – which his lawyer, Rodolfo Yanzon, had used as a reason to argue he couldn’t board a plane back to Italy. Bertulazzi, Yanzon said, suffered three strokes during his two years in detention, and had difficulty walking. He said he told his client on Monday that the judge would not authorise medical testing, however – which he suspects inspired Bertulazzi to flee before he could be extradited. “That was the last thing I said to Bertulazzi,” he added. “He undoubtedly made the decision to prioritise his freedom over his health.”

In an interview with La Repubblica, Bertulazzi’s daughter, Claudia, said he “had no choice” but to flee after an Argentinian court on 3 November rejected his appeal to keep his refugee status, and that he feared spending “the rest of his life in prison” in Italy.

Bertulazzi fled the country in 1980 after being found guilty in the kidnapping of shipowner Pietro Costa, generating a ransom that was allegedly used to fund the Red Brigades’ terrorist activities and to buy a flat in Rome where Moro was held captive. A court in Genoa sentenced him to 27 years in prison.

For years, a complex legal situation meant Bertulazzi could live as a free man in Argentina despite being wanted in Italy. He was arrested in 2002 in Buenos Aires after a joint investigation with Interpol, but was released eight months later because his Italian trials had been held in absentia, preventing his extradition.

Claudi said her father doesn’t fear a retrial: “Partly because, under current laws, we are convinced the only charge that would remain is of participating in an armed group, a charge he has never denied and for which he would accept responsibility.”

She also said she last spoke to her father two days previously and only learned of his escape through the media. “He removed his electronic ankle monitor and lowered himself from the fifth floor using a harness. It’s plausible: he was a mountaineer.”

articles.title: Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in Gaza kills surgeon and five others
articles.summary: Hospital director says 28 wounded in attack on one of few remaining medical facilities in the strip
body: An Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The Israeli military carried out the attack on the hospital, in Khan Younis, early on Thursday saying in a statement it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters there, without providing evidence.

The strike destroyed part of the surgery department, and caused extensive damage to several floors. Services were suspended in four departments: radiology, laboratories, surgical operations and inpatient surgical wards, according to Dr Ahmed al-Fara, hospital director.

The ceiling of one of the wards had caved in, while debris-covered beds lay next to medical instruments twisted from the force of the blast. In other rooms, piles of rubble and shattered concrete cluttered the floor and a hole was left in the floor, where the bomb penetrated the building.

Dr Ayman Abu Ubaid, a surgical specialist at Nasser medical complex, who was wounded in the attack, said: “The bombing caused thick smoke to fill the rooms and fires to break out, amid the groans of wounded and people’s screams. There were many casualties and blood everywhere … Most of us sustained injuries to our limbs, as well as shrapnel wounds in different parts of our bodies.”

Ubaid said the strike came at about 12.30am, without warning. “The patients in the department were all surgical patients waiting to undergo operations. The bombing happened at a time when they should have been asleep,” he said.
Among the dead was Rizk Abu Shaira, 52, a general surgeon who had featured in American Doctor, a documentary about doctors operating in Gaza.

“Dr Rizk was in the American Doctor documentary operating and serving his people. He lost his life doing that, he lost his life because he was doing that,” Dr Thaer Ahmad, who also featured in the documentary, posted on X.
Abu Shaira was killed alongside one of his patients, on whom he had operated.

Nasser hospital is one of the last functioning healthcare facilities in Gaza, after Israeli bombing made most of the strip’s facilities unusable. Last year Israel also struck the hospital, killing five journalists in a double-tap strike on a location often used by reporters for filming. In all, the hospital has been attacked seven times since the war on Gaza began.

The Israeli military has accused Hamas of using hospitals as command centres and to store weapons, an accusation the militant movement rejects. More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed in Gaza, while Doctors Without Borders (MSF) says Israel has detained hundreds of medics since 7 October 2023, with at least 95 still in custody.
About 90% of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damage by Israeli bombing, systematic destruction UN experts called “medicide”.
Attacking healthcare facilities and staff is illegal under international humanitarian law, though these facilities can lose their protected status if they are used for military purposes.
There is an increased need for healthcare during the winter months in Gaza, where rains have displaced people from their tents and increased communicable diseases in crowded encampments.
Already, Nasser hospital is lacking about 80% of its essential medicines and medical supplies, said al-Fara, its director.

One of those killed in Thursday’s strike was Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, 29, who was admitted to Nasser hospital on Monday after a piece of debris fell on his back while he was helping clear rubble from a friend’s home. He was scheduled for surgery at 10am on Thursday, and was meant to receive further treatment abroad.

“Seif was a young man in the prime of his life. He wanted to live, rebuild his home and start a normal life, free from problems and suffering … Seif was killed after already losing two of his brothers and his father. His mother has now lost three of her sons,” said his cousin Tareq Abu Hatab, 37.

Israel launched the war in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack that killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostage. At least 74,645 people have since been killed in Gaza and Israel has carried out a genocide in the strip, according to the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel continues to carry out airstrikes in Gaza, killing more than 1,600 people since the October 2025 “ceasefire”, according to the Gaza ministry of health.

articles.title: ‘Like priests who don’t believe in God’: Italy’s anti-vax medics eye return to frontline duty
articles.summary: Progress of bill to reinstate struck-off doctors hinged on support from far right figure Roberto Vannacci, whose rise is shaping politics before 2027 elections
body: Antonio Cremasco contracted Covid at a dinner party on 6 March 2020. Four days later, as Italy became the first European country to go into nationwide lockdown, he was fighting for his life. “I spent 20 days in intensive care, followed by another 20 days in a hospital ward,” said Cremasco, from Bassano del Grappa in the northern Italian Veneto region.

After leaving hospital, he needed oxygen therapy for another six months. Cremasco’s ordeal was such that when Covid vaccines became available in Italy in early 2021, he had no qualms about being vaccinated, and he believes the decision saved his life once again.
“All those who had been in intensive care with me died,” he said. “Without the vaccine, if I had caught Covid again, I had a high risk of dying too.”
But Cremasco, who is now 76 and recently received his annual Covid and winter flu jab, has struggled to convince his vaccine-sceptic son, a father of two, of the drugs’ safety.

He said he and his wife were wary of having their potentially unvaccinated grandchildren in their home whenever the children were ill, fearing for their own health. “They always seem to be sick,” Cremasco said.
His family rift mirrors a wider divide over vaccination in Italy, which has been brought back to the political spotlight by a controversial bill approved in October in the lower house of parliament.

The measure allows healthcare workers who were struck off their professional registers during the pandemic for serious violations connected to their anti-vaccination beliefs – for example, promoting treatments that lacked a scientific basis – to apply to be reinstated.
The bill is being championed by the prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party and is strongly backed by its far-right coalition partner, the League.

But with allies in Forza Italia split, its approval in the lower house hinged on support from National Future (FN), a rival far-right force led by the former army general Roberto Vannacci, whose emergence is shaping the political landscape before general elections next year.
Vannacci has voiced opposition to vaccine mandates, and his rhetoric frequently targets the vaccine-sceptic audience.

The measure still needs to clear the senate, with a vote scheduled in January. But its progress has alarmed medical experts, less because of the number of healthcare workers involved – it is believed to be very small – and more because of the risk of further eroding trust in vaccines.

Nearly one in two Italian adults are hesitant about vaccination, according to a report by the department of public health and paediatric sciences at the University of Turin published in the Lancet Regional Health Europe in February. The report, which sampled 50,000 adults across Italy, found the ambivalence was driven more by misinformation and lack of institutional trust than by fears over vaccine safety.

“Political communication and the lack of trust among Italians in institutions carry a significant weight,” said Roberta Siliquini, the head of the school of hygiene and preventive medicine at the University of Turin and the report’s chief researcher. “There really is a disinformation campaign in this sense – and those who want to disinform are very good at communicating.”

The implications are being profoundly felt: this year there has been a resurgence in measles, with 472 infections reported during the first five months, compared with 322 in the same period last year, according to health ministry figures. More than half of the cases were reported in young adults. Take-up of the flu vaccine among people aged 65 and over so far this season has dipped to 49.81%, the first time it has fallen below 50% since the winter of 2014-15.

In August, a four-year-old child in Palermo, Sicily, died of diphtheria. Her parents reportedly told doctors they had not vaccinated her because her cousin was autistic and they were convinced vaccines were the reason. There is no evidence of any link between autism and vaccines.

Siquilini said the tragic case was a reminder of the responsibility that everyone, “but especially politicians”, had to deliver the correct message on vaccines. She warned that the rehabilitation of those who rejected scientific evidence could have a “devastating” impact on how people perceived vaccines.
The message has been repeatedly undermined. On 28 October, a day after the lower house vote, Claudio Borghi, a League politician, came under fire for hosting an anti-vaccine seminar in the senate.

Later in the day, in what was believed to have been an indirect rebuke, the Italian president, Sergio Mattarella used a speech during a high-profile cancer research gathering to condemn the spread of anti-vax messages while warning against “irrational beliefs” and “destructive fake news”.

Borghi has proposed revising a law introduced in 2017 by the then leftwing government that extended the number of obligatory childhood vaccinations from four to 10, adding, for example, one against pertussis, or whooping cough. He has defended his position, arguing he is not anti-vaccine but that mandatory vaccines “lead to resistance”.

As for the reinstatement of the medics struck off during the pandemic, he told the Guardian that the proposal’s aim was “to foster reconciliation after all these years”. He said: “In our view, nobody should lose their job because of a personal belief.”

Scepticism over vaccinations took root in Italy in the late 1990s, as in many other countries, mainly driven by now debunked claims of a connection between the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination and autism.
The arrival of social media accelerated the spread of vaccine misinformation, contributing to a drop in immunisation rates against preventable diseases.

The 2017 move to make childhood vaccinations obligatory further emboldened anti-vaccine groups while creating fertile ground for rightwing populist parties, including the Five Star Movement (M5S), which continued to spread misinformation about vaccines after coming to power in 2018, and before the realities of the pandemic forced a shift in tone.
Now in opposition, M5S is highly critical of the move to re-embrace anti-vax healthcare workers.
Lorenzo Mattia Signori, a nurse in Veneto, said politicians were “opportunists” and Meloni’s coalition was simply trying to draw votes from anti-vax voters as it eyed a second mandate.

Signori, who is also a regional secretary for Cittadinanzattiva, an association focused on patient advocacy, including pushing for campaigns to inform citizens about vaccine benefits, said: “Ensuring that people get vaccinated is the largest prevention system we have. If everyone gets sick instead, the Italian healthcare system would not hold.”

He hopes that Mattarella will use his power as president to stop the anti-vaccine medics measure from being signed into law. “We cannot have them in hospitals,” he said. “It would be like going to church and hearing a priest who says he doesn’t believe in God.”

articles.title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang
body: Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.

Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.

UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.

Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.

US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.

Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.

The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …

Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.

There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.

Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.
What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?

The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”

Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).

“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.

China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”
“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.
What approach has the US taken?

Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump. He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.

But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.

The Times writes “Milburn: Cut sick benefits to force young into work”, and the i Paper has “Under-25s with ADHD won’t get £217-a-month benefits in new welfare reforms”.

The FT leads with “Democrats pledge to expose ‘absolute avalanche of corruption’ under Trump”, the Mail has “Even Cameron tells PM: Don’t rejoin the EU”, and the Telegraph writes “SAS issues warning over troop witch hunts”. The Mirror says “Not even a bed for an OAP with cancer”, and the Express has “‘Sanctuary in nature helped me to recover’”.
Trump’s $10bn BBC battle: judge rules lawsuit can go ahead

Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC has been granted permission to proceed, after the corporation’s attempt to get it dismissed was thrown out by a Trump-appointed Florida judge. The case focuses on an edit in a 2024 Panorama documentary that spliced two comments together that were made by the president during a rally before the January 6 Capitol riots, for which the BBC has apologised. With the lawsuit now set to continue, what’s at stake for press freedom? Lucy Hough speaks to global editor, Devika Bhat.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Researchers from the Hoag Family Cancer Institute have made a potential breakthrough in the early diagnosis of ovarian cancer – a disease often detected after it has spread.

For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.

Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.
The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.
